pos: n. (shape, outward appearance; also the essential nature of a thing; rendering Hebrew to'ar, tohu in the negative, Greek morphe, morphosis)
etymology: From Latin forma, shape. The Greek distinction Scripture exploits is between morphe, the form that expresses what a thing truly is, and morphosis, the mere outline or appearance of it — and Paul uses both, of Christ and of hypocrites.
biblical_def: Form in Scripture ranges from bare shape to essential nature, and the most weighty use is Paul's in the Philippian hymn. Christ was in the form of God and “made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men” (Philippians 2:7). The Greek morphe is not costume; it is the outward expression of what a thing genuinely is, which is why the same word can describe His deity and His servanthood without making either a disguise. He did not appear to be God and then appear to be a servant; He was both, and the second was assumed without the first being laid down. Isaiah's servant song sets the paradox in advance: “he hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him” (Isaiah 53:2). Paul then uses the shallower cognate for religion that is all outline: men “having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away” (2 Timothy 3:5) — morphosis, the shape without the substance. And the verb governs the Christian's transformation: “be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind” (Romans 12:2), where the world presses a shape from outside and the Spirit works one from within, at the mind.
webster_summary: Shape, and also essential nature. Christ was in the form of God and took the form of a servant — expression of what He truly is, not costume; the last days have a form of godliness without its power; and the Christian is transformed rather than conformed.
webster_full: FORM, n. [L. forma.] The shape or external appearance of a body; the figure, as defined by lines and angles.
2. Manner of arranging particulars; disposition of particular things.
3. Model; draught; pattern.
4. Beauty; elegance; splendor; dignity. He hath no form nor comeliness. Is. 53.
5. Stated method; established practice; ritual or prescribed mode; as the forms of public worship. A form of godliness. 2 Tim. 3.
scriptures: Philippians 2:7
But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men:
Isaiah 53:2
For he shall grow up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground: he hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him.
2 Timothy 3:5
Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away.
Romans 12:2
And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God.
corruption_summary: 2 Timothy 3:5 is turned against form as such — liturgy, order, and set prayers dismissed as dead formalism — when Paul's complaint is a form emptied of power, not the existence of a form.
corruption_paragraphs: “A form of godliness, but denying the power thereof” is the standing proof-text for a spontaneity that suspects all structure: written prayers are insincere, an order of service quenches the Spirit, and confession recited is confession unfelt. Paul is not making that argument. His subject in 2 Timothy 3 is a catalogue of vices — lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, without natural affection, traitors — held by men who nonetheless keep the outward shape of religion. The problem is the vice, not the shape; and a man of that description is no less dangerous for praying extempore. Scripture is in fact full of prescribed forms: a form of words for the priestly blessing, a psalter for sung worship, and a set prayer given by the Lord Himself with the words when ye pray, say. The regulative principle the dictionary holds is not hostility to form but the conviction that God appoints the forms of His own worship.

The opposite error is the one Paul is actually addressing, and it wears better clothes. A church may hold the confession, keep the calendar, sing the psalms, and administer the ordinances, and be dead — and the outward correctness makes the deadness harder to see, both from outside and from within. This is why the same Scripture that gives the forms insists relentlessly on the reality: circumcision of the heart and not the flesh, a broken and contrite heart rather than sacrifice, the Sabbath kept while the poor are ground. Paul's prescription is not reform of the liturgy but separation from the men — from such turn away. The remedy for a form without power has never been the abolition of the form; it is the return of the power, which is not in the church's gift to manufacture and must be sought where it is given.
roots_summary: Hebrew to'ar (form, outline, comeliness) and tohu (formlessness); Greek morphe (the form expressing essential nature), morphosis (an outline or semblance), and metamorphoo (to transform).
roots_lines: Hebrew to'ar (H8389) — form, outline, figure; the word in Isaiah 53:2 and of Joseph and Rachel being well favoured.
Greek morphe (G3444) — form as the expression of essential nature; used twice in Philippians 2:6-7, of God and of a servant.
Greek morphosis (G3446) — a forming, semblance, outline; the word in 2 Timothy 3:5 and Romans 2:20.
Greek metamorphoo (G3339) — to transform, transfigure; used of Christ on the mount and of the believer in Romans 12:2 and 2 Corinthians 3:18.
Greek syschematizo (G4964) — to conform to a pattern, fashion oneself after; the verb in Romans 12:2 rendered conformed.
usage: “The form of a servant” — morphe, the expression of what He truly became, not a costume worn.
“He hath no form nor comeliness” — nothing in the appearance to account for what He was.
“A form of godliness, but denying the power” — the shape kept and the substance gone.

pos: adj. and adv. (interior, of the hidden man; rendering Hebrew tuchoth, qereb, Greek eso, esothen)
etymology: Old English inweard. Scripture's inward parts are not merely the anatomy but the seat of thought, will, and affection — the place where a man is what he is when no one is looking.
biblical_def: Inward in Scripture names the region God cares about most and man can see least. David states the requirement after his adultery: “Behold, thou desirest truth in the inward parts: and in the hidden part thou shalt make me to know wisdom” (Psalm 51:6). The demand and the promise are joined — God requires truth where a man cannot manufacture it, and undertakes to teach wisdom there Himself. The principle is stated to Samuel at the anointing of David, and it corrects a prophet: “the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7). Paul then uses the inward man for the regenerate self in two of the most honest sentences in his writings. In Romans 7 it is the seat of a genuine delight that his members contradict: “I delight in the law of God after the inward man” (Romans 7:22). In 2 Corinthians it is the part of him that is going the opposite direction from his body: “though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16). Two processes run at once in every Christian — a visible decay and an invisible renewal — and only one of them will be reported by a mirror.
webster_summary: The hidden man. God desires truth in the inward parts and looks on the heart where man looks on the outward appearance; Paul delights in God's law after the inward man, and reports that it is renewed daily while the outward man perishes.
webster_full: INWARD, a. [Sax. inweard.] Internal; interior; placed or being within.
2. Intimate; domestic; familiar.
3. Seated in the mind or soul; as inward joy or grief.
INWARD, adv. Toward the inside; as, to bend a thing inward.
INWARDS, n. plu. The bowels; the intestines; and figuratively, the seat of the affections. Truth in the inward parts. Ps. 51.
scriptures: Psalm 51:6
Behold, thou desirest truth in the inward parts: and in the hidden part thou shalt make me to know wisdom.
1 Samuel 16:7

But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.
Romans 7:22
For I delight in the law of God after the inward man:
2 Corinthians 4:16
For which cause we faint not; but though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day.
corruption_summary: The biblical inwardness — a heart God searches, requires truth in, and renews — has been replaced by an inwardness that is self-authenticating, in which the inner life is consulted as an oracle rather than examined as a defendant.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern spirituality is intensely inward and almost never self-suspecting. It looks in to find the true self, the authentic desire, the inner voice, and it treats what it finds as evidence. Psalm 51 goes inward in the opposite spirit: David asks God to look, because he cannot trust his own report, and the psalm ends by asking for a clean heart to be created rather than uncovered. Jeremiah 17:9-10 states the same logic — the heart is deceitful and unsearchable by its owner, and the LORD searches it. The difference is not in the direction of attention but in who is authorised to give the verdict. An inwardness that consults itself will always ratify itself; an inwardness that submits to being searched can actually be changed.

The opposite corruption is the outward religion that 1 Samuel 16:7 was spoken against, and it survives everywhere. Churches still weigh countenance and stature — presence, articulacy, success, the family that photographs well — and Samuel, a genuine prophet, was doing it in that very verse until God stopped him. What Scripture puts in place of appearance is not indifference to the visible but a different order of evidence: fruit over time, faithfulness in what is least, conduct in the household, and reputation among outsiders, all of which are slow and none of which impress at first sight. Paul's 2 Corinthians 4:16 is the pastoral pay-off. A man whose worth is located in the outward man is on a losing schedule, since the outward man is perishing on a fixed timetable; a man being renewed inwardly gets better as he gets worse.
roots_summary: Hebrew tuchoth (the inward parts, from a root meaning to overlay or coat) and qereb (the midst, inner part); Greek eso (within) and esothen (from within), with ho eso anthropos, the inward man.
roots_lines: Hebrew tuchoth (H2910) — the inward parts; a rare word, used in Psalm 51:6 and Job 38:36.
Hebrew qereb (H7130) — the midst, inward part; used of the new spirit put within in Ezekiel 36:26-27.
Hebrew lebab (H3824) — heart, inner man; what the LORD looks on in 1 Samuel 16:7.
Greek eso (G2080) — within, inner; in the phrase ho eso anthropos, the inward man (Romans 7:22; 2 Corinthians 4:16; Ephesians 3:16).
Greek anakainoo (G341) — to renew, make new again; the verb in 2 Corinthians 4:16, in the present passive: is being renewed.
usage: “Thou desirest truth in the inward parts” — required where a man cannot manufacture it, and given by the God who requires it.
“Man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart” — spoken to correct a prophet in the act.
“The inward man is renewed day by day” — two processes at once, and only one shows in a mirror.

pos: v.t. (to apprehend by sense or understanding; rendering Hebrew bin, yada, Greek ginosko, noeo)
etymology: From Latin percipere, to seize thoroughly — per, through, and capere, to take. Perception in Scripture is a grasping, and its absence is not a defect of the eyes but a judgment on the heart.
biblical_def: To perceive is to take in and grasp, and Scripture's most important use of the word is negative. Isaiah's commission is a sentence of judicial blindness: “Go, and tell this people, Hear ye indeed, but understand not; and see ye indeed, but perceive not” (Isaiah 6:9). The seeing is real and the perceiving does not follow, because the fault lies behind the eye; the Lord Jesus quotes this text to explain why He teaches in parables, and it is cited in all four Gospels and in Acts — the New Testament's most repeated Old Testament quotation. Against that stands perception granted. Peter, having seen a vision and walked into a Gentile house, says: “Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons” (Acts 10:34) — a man reaching a conclusion he had resisted for years, in a single moment, with God's help. The Lord Jesus uses the word of His own knowledge in the press of a crowd: “Somebody hath touched me: for I perceive that virtue is gone out of me” (Luke 8:46). And Job supplies the honest experience of the believer who is not being given perception: “Lo, he goeth by me, and I see him not: he passeth on also, but I perceive him not” (Job 9:11). God is there and passing by, and a righteous man cannot make Him out.
webster_summary: To grasp by sense or understanding. Isaiah's commission is a sentence of judicial blindness — see, and perceive not — quoted more than any other Old Testament text in the New; Peter perceives what he had long resisted; Job cannot make God out at all.
webster_full: PERCEIVE, v.t. [L. percipio; per and capio, to take.] To have knowledge or receive impressions of external objects through the medium of the senses.
2. To know; to understand; to observe.
3. To be affected by; to receive impressions from.
PERCEPTION, n. The act of perceiving or of receiving impressions by the senses.
4. Discernment; knowledge. See ye indeed, but perceive not. Is. 6.
scriptures: Isaiah 6:9
And he said, Go, and tell this people, Hear ye indeed, but understand not; and see ye indeed, but perceive not.
Acts 10:34
Then Peter opened his mouth, and said, Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons:
Luke 8:46
And Jesus said, Somebody hath touched me: for I perceive that virtue is gone out of me.
Job 9:11
Lo, he goeth by me, and I see him not: he passeth on also, but I perceive him not.
corruption_summary: Isaiah 6:9 is softened into a description of people who happen not to be paying attention, so that unbelief becomes an information problem — and the doctrine of spiritual inability, which the text and its six New Testament citations teach, is set aside.
corruption_paragraphs: The instinct of most modern evangelism is that unbelief is a failure of communication: explain more clearly, illustrate better, remove the obstacles, and perception will follow. Isaiah 6:9 says something harder. The people hear indeed and see indeed — the transmission is not the problem — and understanding does not result, and the prophet is sent knowing it will not. Paul states the doctrine plainly: the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God, neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned (1 Corinthians 2:14). This is not a reason for poor preaching or for fatalism; Isaiah still went, and preached for decades. It is the reason preaching must be accompanied by prayer for what preaching cannot produce. A clarity that could of itself create perception would make the new birth unnecessary, and John 3 would be a misunderstanding.

The mirror error is to take the doctrine of inability as an excuse for obscurity or for a shrug at the lost. Paul, who wrote 1 Corinthians 2:14, also renounced the hidden things of dishonesty and commended himself to every man's conscience by manifestation of the truth (2 Corinthians 4:2), and pressed men with tears. Peter's of a truth I perceive is worth setting beside Isaiah's commission for exactly this reason: perception is granted, and it was granted to a man who had been shown a vision three times and still argued. The preacher's duty is plain speech and plain pleading; the granting of sight is God's, and Job's complaint stands as permission for the believer who is temporarily given neither.
roots_summary: Hebrew bin (to discern, understand) and yada (to know); Greek ginosko (to come to know), noeo (to perceive with the mind), and epiginosko (to know fully, recognise).
roots_lines: Hebrew bin (H995) — to discern, consider, understand; the verb in Isaiah 6:9 rendered understand not.
Hebrew yada (H3045) — to know, perceive by experience; the broad Hebrew term for knowledge, including covenantal knowing.
Greek ginosko (G1097) — to know, come to know; the verb in Luke 8:46 and John 12:19.
Greek noeo (G3539) — to perceive with the mind, consider; used in Matthew 15:17 and Hebrews 11:3.
Greek katalambano (G2638) — to lay hold of, apprehend; the verb in Acts 10:34 rendered I perceive, and in John 1:5 of the darkness not comprehending the light.
usage: “See ye indeed, but perceive not” — the transmission is fine; the fault is behind the eye.
“Of a truth I perceive” — a man reaching in one moment a conclusion he had resisted for years.
“He passeth on also, but I perceive him not” — God present and passing by, and a righteous man missing Him.

pos: adj. (wonderful, exciting astonishment; rendering Hebrew pala, Greek thaumastos)
etymology: From Old French merveillos, from Latin mirabilis, wonderful, from mirari, to wonder at. The KJV spelling doubles the l. The Hebrew pala means to be extraordinary or beyond a man's power — the marvellous is what men could not have done.
biblical_def: Marvellous describes what lies beyond human power, and its most consequential use is in a psalm about a rejected stone: “The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner. This is the LORD's doing; it is marvellous in our eyes” (Psalm 118:22-23). The Lord Jesus quotes it to the chief priests as they are deciding to kill Him, and asks whether they had ever read it: “The stone which the builders rejected, the same is become the head of the corner: this is the Lord's doing, and it is marvellous in our eyes” (Matthew 21:42). The men rejecting the stone are told in advance that their rejection is the mechanism of the exaltation, and that God's hand in it will be the wonder of the ages. Peter uses the word for what conversion is a passage into: believers are a chosen generation and a royal priesthood, called “out of darkness into his marvellous light” (1 Peter 2:9) — and Peter, in the same passage, calls Christ that same rejected stone. David turns the word on his own body: “I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well” (Psalm 139:14). The marvellous in Scripture is not chiefly the spectacular; it is God's doing, whether in a corner-stone, a conversion, or the knitting of a body in secret.
webster_summary: Beyond human power. The rejected stone made head of the corner is the LORD's doing and marvellous in our eyes, quoted by Christ to the men rejecting Him; Peter calls conversion a call into marvellous light; David calls his own body marvellous work.
webster_full: MARVELOUS, MARVELLOUS, a. [Fr. merveilleux.] Wonderful; strange; exciting wonder or some degree of surprise.
2. Surpassing credit; incredible.
3. The marvelous, in writings, is that which exceeds natural power, or is preternatural; opposed to probable.
MARVEL, n. A wonder; that which arrests the attention and causes a person to stand or gaze, or to pause.
5. This is the Lord's doing; it is marvelous in our eyes. Ps. 118.
scriptures: Psalm 118:23
This is the LORD'S doing; it is marvellous in our eyes.
Matthew 21:42

Jesus saith unto them, Did ye never read in the scriptures, The stone which the builders rejected, the same is become the head of the corner: this is the Lord's doing, and it is marvellous in our eyes?
1 Peter 2:9
But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:
Psalm 139:14
I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well.
corruption_summary: The word has been worn down into a general term of enthusiasm, so that the category Scripture reserves for what only God could have done is spent on preferences and performances — and Psalm 139:14 is detached from the God whose work it credits.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the loss is one of currency rather than of doctrine. Marvellous in Scripture translates pala, which means to be extraordinary, difficult, beyond a man's reach — the same root that asks whether anything is too hard for the LORD (Genesis 18:14). When the word is spent on a meal, a holiday, and a singer within the same hour, the vocabulary for what only God can do quietly disappears, and with it the habit of noticing. Psalm 118:23 is precise about this: the marvel is not the corner-stone's beauty but its provenance — this is the LORD's doing. The principle to recover is that the marvellous is identified by its author rather than by the intensity of the impression it makes, which is why a conversion is more marvellous than a spectacle.

Psalm 139:14 has met a related fate. “Fearfully and wonderfully made” circulates widely as an affirmation of self-worth, and it is generally quoted without the clause that follows or the psalm that surrounds it. The verse is addressed to God, not to the self — I will praise thee — and the wonder is His workmanship in the womb, described in the next verses as being wrought in secret and written in His book before there was any of it. That makes the psalm one of Scripture's strongest statements on the personhood of the unborn, and it grounds human dignity where it can bear weight: not in a person's estimate of himself, which will fluctuate, but in the fact that he was made deliberately by a God who was watching.
roots_summary: Hebrew pala (to be extraordinary, beyond power) and niphla'oth (wondrous works); Greek thaumastos (marvellous, wonderful) and thaumazo (to marvel).
roots_lines: Hebrew pala (H6381) — to be extraordinary, beyond one's power; the root in Psalm 118:23 and in Genesis 18:14.
Hebrew niphla'oth (H6381 participle) — wondrous works; the standard Psalter term for God's acts in redemption and creation.
Greek thaumastos (G2298) — marvellous, wonderful; the word in Matthew 21:42 and 1 Peter 2:9.
Greek thaumazo (G2296) — to wonder, marvel; used of the crowds, and notably of Christ marvelling at unbelief (Mark 6:6) and at faith (Matthew 8:10).
Hebrew rosh pinnah — head of the corner; the architectural term in Psalm 118:22 applied to Christ throughout the New Testament.
usage: “This is the LORD'S doing” — the marvel is identified by its author, not by the impression it makes.
“Out of darkness into his marvellous light” — conversion as the passage into the marvellous.
“I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made” — addressed to God, and about His workmanship.

pos: v.i. and n. (familiar speech, conversation; rendering Hebrew dabar, siach, Greek laleo, homileo)
etymology: Middle English talken, a frequentative of tell. Scripture treats ordinary conversation with a seriousness the word's casualness disguises — it is the medium of household discipleship, and it is entered as evidence at the judgment.
biblical_def: Talk is ordinary conversation, and Scripture assigns it two roles: it is the chief instrument of raising children in the faith, and it is evidence at the last day. The Shema's instruction to Israel places doctrine in the flow of household life rather than in a classroom: “thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up” (Deuteronomy 6:7). Four settings, covering the whole day, none of them formal. The Lord Jesus then puts unconsidered speech into the record: “every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment” (Matthew 12:36) — idle meaning unemployed, thrown off, the words a man would not defend and does not remember. Paul gives the positive rule with an economy that leaves no room for the usual exemptions: “Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers” (Ephesians 4:29). The test is not whether speech is true but whether it builds and whether it gives grace to those who hear. And Job's friend Zophar, wrong about much, is right about this: “should a man full of talk be justified?” (Job 11:2).
webster_summary: Ordinary conversation, and Scripture takes it seriously. Deuteronomy makes talk the medium of household discipleship across the whole day; Christ says idle words are accounted for; Paul requires speech that edifies and ministers grace to hearers.
webster_full: TALK, v.i. tauk. To converse familiarly; to speak, as in familiar discourse, when two or more persons interchange thoughts.
2. To prate; to speak impertinently.
3. To talk of, to relate; to tell; to give an account of.
TALK, n. Familiar converse; mutual discourse; that which is uttered by one person in familiar conversation.
5. Subject of discourse; as, this is the talk of the town. Shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house. Deut. 6.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 6:7
And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
Matthew 12:36
But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment.
Ephesians 4:29
Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers.
Job 11:2
Should not the multitude of words be answered? and should a man full of talk be justified?
corruption_summary: Speech has been reclassified as harmless in itself — talk is just talk, and only actions count — at the same time that a rival error treats certain words as harmful in a nearly magical sense, with both readings missing what Scripture actually weighs.
corruption_paragraphs: The first assumption is the folk wisdom that words are cheap and deeds are what matter. Scripture treats speech as a principal work, not a substitute for one. The tongue is a fire and a world of iniquity, defiling the whole body (James 3:6); by thy words thou shalt be justified and by thy words condemned (Matthew 12:37); death and life are in the power of the tongue (Proverbs 18:21). Christ's reason in Matthew 12 is diagnostic: out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh, so unguarded talk is the most reliable available sample of the inner man — which is precisely why the idle word, not the prepared statement, is the one entered in evidence. A church that disciplines for adultery and tolerates a slanderous tongue for thirty years has not read the epistles it preaches from.

The opposite error inflates certain words into contaminants whose mere utterance injures, and it usually arrives with a list. Scripture's categories are different and more searching. Ephesians 4:29 does not supply a vocabulary of forbidden terms; it applies a functional test — does this build up, and does it give grace to the hearers? — which condemns a great deal of perfectly polite speech: the accurate report that damages, the joke at a brother's expense, the theological correction delivered to wound. And Deuteronomy 6:7 supplies the positive charge that most households neglect. Faith is transmitted mainly through unscheduled talk — sitting, walking, lying down, rising up — which means a father who outsources his children's instruction entirely to a Sunday programme has not delegated the duty but declined it.
roots_summary: Hebrew dabar (to speak) and siach (to muse, converse); Greek laleo (to speak, utter), homileo (to converse — the root of homily), and logos (word, account).
roots_lines: Hebrew dabar (H1696) — to speak, talk; the verb in Deuteronomy 6:7 and the root of dabar, a word or thing.
Hebrew siach (H7878) — to muse, meditate, talk; the verb in Psalm 119:15 and 1 Chronicles 16:9.
Greek laleo (G2980) — to speak, utter; the ordinary verb of speech, distinct from lego, to say with content.
Greek homileo (G3656) — to converse, talk with; used of the two on the Emmaus road (Luke 24:14-15).
Greek argos (G692) — idle, unemployed, unproductive; the adjective in Matthew 12:36, the same word rendered barren in 2 Peter 1:8.
usage: “Shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house” — four settings covering the whole day, none of them formal.
“Every idle word… they shall give account” — the unguarded word is the most reliable sample of the heart.
“That it may minister grace unto the hearers” — the test is not truth alone but whether it builds.

pos: v.t. (to number; also to reckon or account something to be so; rendering Hebrew chashab, manah, Greek logizomai, hegeomai)
etymology: From Old French conter, Latin computare, to reckon. The two English senses — to enumerate and to consider — are both in Scripture, and the second carries the doctrine of imputation.
biblical_def: To count is both to enumerate and to reckon a thing to be so, and the second sense is theologically decisive. It is the word behind imputation: Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness (Romans 4:3), where the Greek logizomai is a bookkeeping term — something is entered to an account that was not there before. Paul then applies the same verb to his own ledger, counting his considerable religious assets as loss for Christ. In the plainer sense, the Lord Jesus makes counting a duty of discipleship: “which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?” (Luke 14:28) — a warning against following Him on an unexamined impulse, delivered to great multitudes rather than to hesitant enquirers. James commands a reckoning that runs against the grain of the senses: “count it all joy when ye fall into divers temptations” (James 1:2), which is not the pretence that trials are pleasant but the deliberate entry of them on the right side of the ledger, on the stated ground that trying works patience. Moses asks for the arithmetic that produces wisdom: “So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom” (Psalm 90:12). And Balaam, of all people, wishes for an end he will not have: “Who can count the dust of Jacob…? Let me die the death of the righteous” (Numbers 23:10).
webster_summary: To number, and to reckon a thing to be so. The second sense carries imputation. Christ requires counting the cost before following; James commands counting trials as joy; Moses asks to number his days; Balaam wishes for a righteous man's death.
webster_full: COUNT, v.t. [Fr. compter; L. computo; con and puto, to throw together.] To number; to tell or name one by one, for ascertaining the whole number of units in a collection.
2. To reckon; to preserve a reckoning; to compute.
3. To esteem; to account; to reckon; to think, judge, or consider. I count them but dung. Phil. 3.
4. To impute; to charge. It was counted to him for righteousness. Rom. 4.
COUNT, n. Reckoning; the act of numbering; as, this is the number according to my count.
scriptures: Luke 14:28
For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?
James 1:2
My brethren, count it all joy when ye fall into divers temptations;
Psalm 90:12
So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.
Numbers 23:10
Who can count the dust of Jacob, and the number of the fourth part of Israel? Let me die the death of the righteous, and let my last end be like his!
corruption_summary: “Count the cost” has been detached from the discipleship it introduces and turned into generic prudential advice — while James 1:2 is preached as a demand for cheerfulness in suffering that the verse does not make.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke 14:28 is quoted in stewardship seminars and business talks as counsel about planning, and the parable does teach that. But the Lord Jesus tells it in the middle of the most severe passage on discipleship in the Gospels: whoever does not hate father and mother and his own life also cannot be His disciple; whoever bears not his cross cannot be His disciple; and the paragraph closes, so likewise, whosoever he be of you that forsaketh not all that he hath, he cannot be my disciple (Luke 14:33). The tower and the king going to war are illustrations of that, and they are addressed to great multitudes who were following Him easily. He is thinning a crowd on purpose. Preaching that reduces the passage to prudence has performed the opposite operation from the one the passage exists to perform.

James 1:2 suffers a different distortion, and it wounds people. Preached as a command to feel joy in affliction, it makes a grieving Christian guilty for grieving, and it flatly contradicts the Bible's own record — the Psalms of lament, the Lord weeping at Lazarus's tomb, Paul's sorrow upon sorrow at Epaphroditus's illness. Count is hegeomai, to reckon, to judge a thing to be the case. James is commanding a verdict, not a feeling: the trial is producing patience, patience is producing completeness, and the believer is to enter it on the ledger accordingly while it still hurts. That is a demand on the mind, made available to the man who is weeping, and it is far more useful to him than an instruction to stop.
roots_summary: Hebrew chashab (to reckon, impute, account) and manah (to number, apportion); Greek logizomai (to reckon, the imputation word), hegeomai (to consider, deem), and psephizo (to count with pebbles, the verb in Luke 14:28).
roots_lines: Hebrew chashab (H2803) — to reckon, impute, account; the verb in Genesis 15:6, counted it to him for righteousness.
Hebrew manah (H4487) — to number, count out, appoint; used of numbering days and of God appointing the great fish.
Greek logizomai (G3049) — to reckon, credit to an account; the technical term of imputation in Romans 4.
Greek hegeomai (G2233) — to lead, consider, deem; the verb in James 1:2 and Philippians 3:7-8.
Greek psephizo (G5585) — to count with pebbles, calculate; the verb in Luke 14:28 and Revelation 13:18.
usage: “Counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish” — told to great multitudes, to thin them.
“Count it all joy” — a verdict commanded of the mind, not a feeling demanded of the heart.
“Teach us to number our days” — the arithmetic that produces wisdom.

pos: n. (an instant of time; rendering Hebrew rega, Greek atomos, parautika)
etymology: From Latin momentum, a movement, and by extension the smallest measurable interval — the instant in which a balance tips. The Greek in 1 Corinthians 15:52 is atomos, that which cannot be cut: an indivisible instant.
biblical_def: A moment in Scripture is the smallest unit of time, and it is used to measure two things against one another: the brevity of wrath and affliction, and the suddenness of God's decisive acts. On the first, the psalmist sets a divine ratio: “his anger endureth but a moment; in his favour is life: weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning” (Psalm 30:5). Isaiah counsels the same patience under judgment — “hide thyself as it were for a little moment, until the indignation be overpast” (Isaiah 26:20). Paul weighs the whole of Christian suffering on that scale and finds it light: “our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory” (2 Corinthians 4:17) — written by a man beaten, stoned, shipwrecked, and imprisoned, who is not minimising anything but comparing. The moment is also the unit of God's decisive action, and the resurrection is timed in it: “In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed” (1 Corinthians 15:52). The Greek atomos means indivisible — there will be no process, no interval, nothing to observe partway through. The same instant that measures the brevity of grief measures the speed of glory.
webster_summary: The smallest unit of time. God's anger endures a moment where His favour is life; Paul weighs all Christian affliction as light and momentary against eternal glory; and the resurrection happens in an atomos, an indivisible instant.
webster_full: MOMENT, n. [L. momentum, from moveo, to move.] The most minute and indivisible part of time; an instant.
2. Force; impulse; impulsive power.
3. Importance in influence or effect; consequence; weight or value; as a matter of moment.
MOMENTARY, a. Lasting but a moment; done in a moment.
5. In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye. 1 Cor. 15.
scriptures: 2 Corinthians 4:17
For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory;
1 Corinthians 15:52
In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed.
Psalm 30:5
For his anger endureth but a moment; in his favour is life: weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning.
Isaiah 26:20
Come, my people, enter thou into thy chambers, and shut thy doors about thee: hide thyself as it were for a little moment, until the indignation be overpast.
corruption_summary: 2 Corinthians 4:17 is used to hurry the grieving past their grief — your affliction is light and momentary, so stop — which turns Paul's comparison into a dismissal he never made.
corruption_paragraphs: The verse is regularly deployed at the wrong moment and with the wrong force, as a rebuke to a Christian whose suffering is not resolving on schedule. Two things are worth noticing about who wrote it. Paul's catalogue in the same letter — stripes above measure, prisons, deaths oft, five times forty stripes save one, thrice beaten with rods, once stoned, thrice shipwrecked (2 Corinthians 11:23-25) — means light affliction is not the verdict of a comfortable man. And the same letter contains his admission that he was pressed out of measure, above strength, insomuch that he despaired even of life (2 Corinthians 1:8). The comparison is between two real weights, not a denial that one of them is heavy. Psalm 30:5 shows the right pastoral use: weeping may endure for a night, and the night is granted, named, and not hurried. The believer who is told his grief should already be over has been given the arithmetic without the permission.

There is a second-order misuse in eschatology, where 1 Corinthians 15:52 has been made the anchor text of a secret rapture and a detailed timetable. Paul's in a moment is a statement about the manner of the change, not the schedule of it, and its immediate context is a trumpet, the raising of the dead, and the swallowing up of death in victory — the public and final end. The dictionary holds the bodily second coming, the resurrection of the just and the unjust, and the final judgment, and declines the dispensational scheme that arranges these into stages the New Testament nowhere separates. What the verse gives the believer is better than a timetable: however long the night, the change itself will take no time at all.
roots_summary: Hebrew rega (an instant, a wink), from a root meaning to blink; Greek atomos (indivisible, hence an instant), rhipe (a flick, as of the eye), and parautika (momentary, for the present).
roots_lines: Hebrew rega (H7281) — a moment, instant; the word in Psalm 30:5, Isaiah 26:20, and Isaiah 54:7-8.
Greek atomos (G823) — uncut, indivisible; the noun in 1 Corinthians 15:52 and the source of the English atom.
Greek rhipe (G4493) — a flick, jerk, twinkling; joined to ophthalmos (eye) in the same verse.
Greek parautika (G3910) — for the present, momentary; the adverb in 2 Corinthians 4:17.
Greek baros (G922) — weight, burden; the noun Paul sets against the lightness, an eternal weight of glory.
usage: “Light affliction, which is but for a moment” — written by a man five times scourged; a comparison, not a dismissal.
“In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye” — atomos, indivisible; there will be nothing to observe partway through.
“Weeping may endure for a night” — the night is granted, named, and not hurried.

pos: n. and v. (knowledge, understanding; in the archaic idiom to wit, namely; rendering Hebrew yada, Greek in explanatory apposition)
etymology: Old English witan, to know — the same root as German wissen and English wise. In the KJV wit almost never means humour; it means knowledge, and its commonest use is the connective to wit, meaning namely.
biblical_def: Wit in the Authorized Version is knowledge, and it is one of the archaisms most likely to trip a modern reader. Its dominant use is the connective phrase to wit, meaning namely or that is to say, and it introduces some of the New Testament's weightiest clauses. Paul defines reconciliation with it: “To wit, that God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto himself, not imputing their trespasses unto them; and hath committed unto us the word of reconciliation” (2 Corinthians 5:19). He defines the object of the creation's groaning with it: believers groan within themselves, “waiting for the adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body” (Romans 8:23) — a clause that fixes Christian hope on a bodily and not a merely spiritual future. As a verb of knowing it appears in the narratives: Abraham's servant “held his peace, to wit whether the LORD had made his journey prosperous or not” (Genesis 24:21), watching in silence to learn the answer; and Miriam “stood afar off, to wit what would be done to him” (Exodus 2:4), a girl waiting beside a river to find out whether her brother would live. And the Psalter gives the idiom the modern ear knows best, of sailors in a storm: “They reel to and fro, and stagger like a drunken man, and are at their wits' end” (Psalm 107:27) — the end of knowing, where the next verse has them cry unto the LORD.
webster_summary: Knowledge, not humour. To wit means namely, and it introduces the definition of reconciliation and of the adoption we await; as a verb it is the silent watching of Abraham's servant and of Miriam; wits' end is where sailors begin to pray.
webster_full: WIT, v.t. or i. [Sax. witan, to know.] To know; obsolete except in the phrase, to wit, that is, to know, namely, videlicet.
2. WIT, n. Primarily, the intellect; the understanding or mental powers.
3. The association of ideas in a manner natural and pleasing, but unexpected.
4. A man of genius; as, the wits of the age.
5. Wits, in the plural, soundness of mind; intellect; as, at his wits' end. Ps. 107.
scriptures: 2 Corinthians 5:19
To wit, that God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto himself, not imputing their trespasses unto them; and hath committed unto us the word of reconciliation.
Romans 8:23
And not only they, but ourselves also, which have the firstfruits of the Spirit, even we ourselves groan within ourselves, waiting for the adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body.
Genesis 24:21
And the man wondering at her held his peace, to wit whether the LORD had made his journey prosperous or not.
Psalm 107:27
They reel to and fro, and stagger like a drunken man, and are at their wits' end.
corruption_summary: The archaism is simply lost on modern readers, who hear wit as cleverness or humour and so skip past the connective that introduces some of Scripture's most compact doctrinal statements.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the problem is linguistic drift, and it costs the reader something specific. To wit is an apposition marker: what follows is not an addition but a definition of what preceded. Miss it in 2 Corinthians 5:19 and the verse becomes a general statement about reconciliation; catch it and the verse is defining the ministry Paul has just described, and doing so in the most precise language available — God was in Christ, reconciling, not imputing their trespasses. That last clause is the negative side of imputation, and it is joined to the positive in the following verse: He was made sin for us, that we might be made the righteousness of God in Him. The whole doctrine of the great exchange stands in a sentence introduced by an archaism most readers slide over.

Romans 8:23 rewards the same attention and corrects a common error. Christians frequently speak of the believer's hope as escape from the body, and much popular piety is functionally Platonic — the soul released, the body left behind, heaven as disembodiment. Paul says the thing waited for is the adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body. The apposition rules out any reading in which the body is dispensable; the creation itself groans for the same deliverance, and the resurrection of the flesh is in every catholic creed. Recovering the small connective recovers the doctrine: what a Christian awaits is not a better afterlife but a raised body in a renewed world, and the vocabulary of Scripture is careful about it even where its English has gone quiet.
roots_summary: Old English witan, to know, cognate with Latin videre and Greek oida; the phrase to wit renders Hebrew lada'ath (to know) and Greek appositional constructions, and corresponds to the Latin videlicet.
roots_lines: Old English witan — to know; the root of wit, wise, wisdom, and the archaic wist (knew) and wot (knows).
Hebrew yada (H3045) — to know; the verb rendered to wit in Genesis 24:21 and Exodus 2:4.
Greek hos hoti — the appositional construction in 2 Corinthians 5:19 that the KJV renders to wit.
Latin videlicet — namely, to wit; the legal Latin equivalent, abbreviated viz.
Greek apolytrosis (G629) — redemption, a buying back; the noun the apposition defines in Romans 8:23.
usage: “To wit, that God was in Christ” — not an addition but a definition of the reconciliation just named.
“The adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body” — the apposition that rules out a disembodied hope.
“At their wits' end” — the end of knowing, and the verse before men cry unto the LORD.

pos: n. and v.t. (one who leads the way; to conduct; rendering Hebrew nachah, alluph, Greek hodegeo)
etymology: From Old French guider. The Greek hodegeo is built from hodos, a road, and hegeomai, to lead — to lead along a road, which is exactly what Scripture means: guidance is conduct along a way, not the disclosure of a map.
biblical_def: To guide is to lead along a road, and Scripture assigns the office to God, to His Spirit, and to men who teach. The Psalter's claim is total and unhedged: “For this God is our God for ever and ever: he will be our guide even unto death” (Psalm 48:14) — not to the edge of death, but unto it and through the last stretch where no other guide can come. Isaiah gives the promise its most generous form, and attaches it to the fast of mercy in chapter 58: “the LORD shall guide thee continually, and satisfy thy soul in drought, and make fat thy bones: and thou shalt be like a watered garden” (Isaiah 58:11). The Lord Jesus promises the Spirit in the same terms, with a striking limitation on His manner: “when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will guide you into all truth: for he shall not speak of himself; but whatsoever he shall hear, that shall he speak” (John 16:13). The Spirit is a guide who speaks nothing on His own authority — which is why the Spirit's guidance never contradicts the word He gave. And Scripture is candid that God ordinarily guides through people: the Ethiopian, reading Isaiah in his chariot, answers Philip's question with one of his own — “How can I, except some man should guide me?” (Acts 8:31).
webster_summary: To lead along a road. God is His people's guide even unto death and guides continually; the Spirit guides into all truth while speaking nothing of Himself; and the Ethiopian's question — how can I, except some man should guide me? — is why teachers exist.
webster_full: GUIDE, v.t. [Fr. guider.] To lead or direct in a way; to conduct in a course or path; to pilot; as, to guide an army.
2. To direct; to order; to influence; to superintend.
3. To instruct and direct; as, to guide the young.
GUIDE, n. A person who leads or directs another in his way or course; a conductor.
5. A director; a regulator; that which leads or conducts. He will be our guide even unto death. Ps. 48.
scriptures: Psalm 48:14
For this God is our God for ever and ever: he will be our guide even unto death.
John 16:13

Howbeit when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will guide you into all truth: for he shall not speak of himself; but whatsoever he shall hear, that shall he speak: and he will shew you things to come.
Isaiah 58:11
And the LORD shall guide thee continually, and satisfy thy soul in drought, and make fat thy bones: and thou shalt be like a watered garden, and like a spring of water, whose waters fail not.
Psalm 73:24
Thou shalt guide me with thy counsel, and afterward receive me to glory.
corruption_summary: Divine guidance has been reduced to a technique for extracting decisions — open doors, inner impressions, fleeces — and John 16:13, a promise to the apostles concerning the giving of the New Testament, is treated as a warrant for private revelations that add to it.
corruption_paragraphs: Most evangelical anxiety about guidance concerns decisions Scripture does not address: which job, which house, which person. The machinery invented to settle them — open and closed doors, peace as a verdict, fleeces laid in imitation of a passage that presents Gideon's fleece as unbelief rather than method — produces Christians who are perpetually uncertain and unusually easy to manipulate, since anyone claiming a word from the Lord outranks argument. Scripture's own model of guidance is a road walked: the word is a lamp unto my feet and a light unto my path (Psalm 119:105), which illuminates the next step rather than the whole route. God guides by making a man wise, and He makes him wise through the Scriptures, the counsel of the godly, providential circumstance, and sanctified reason. Where the Bible has not spoken, a Christian is free, and freedom is not a failure of guidance.

John 16:13 is the load-bearing text for the other error, and its addressees matter. The Lord Jesus is speaking to the eleven in the upper room, promising that the Spirit will bring to their remembrance whatsoever He has said to them (John 14:26) and guide them into all truth — a promise of the apostolic deposit, that is, of the New Testament itself. Read as a general promise of ongoing revelation, it becomes a standing warrant for whatever any believer feels guided to, and the church has no defence against it. Note also the limitation the verse itself imposes: the Spirit shall not speak of Himself. Any alleged guidance that contradicts, supplements, or outranks the written word therefore fails on the terms of the very verse claimed for it, since the Spirit does not speak against what He has already said.
roots_summary: Hebrew nachah (to lead, guide) and alluph (a familiar friend, guide); Greek hodegeo (to lead along a road, from hodos, a way) and hodegos (a guide, used of the blind guides of Matthew 23).
roots_lines: Hebrew nachah (H5148) — to lead, guide, conduct; the verb in Psalm 23:3, Psalm 73:24, and Isaiah 58:11.
Hebrew nahal (H5095) — to lead gently, as flocks with young; used in Isaiah 40:11 and Psalm 23:2.
Greek hodegeo (G3594) — to lead along a road, guide; the verb in John 16:13 and Acts 8:31.
Greek hodegos (G3595) — a guide, leader of the way; used of Judas in Acts 1:16 and of the blind guides in Matthew 23:16, 24.
Greek hodos (G3598) — a road, way; the root, and the earliest name for Christianity itself (Acts 9:2).
usage: “Our guide even unto death” — unto it and through it, where no other guide can come.
“He shall not speak of himself” — the limitation the Spirit accepts, and the test of every claimed guidance.
“How can I, except some man should guide me?” — why God gives teachers, and why Philip was sent.

pos: n. (public report, renown; rendering Hebrew shema, shemuah, Greek pheme, akoe)
etymology: From Latin fama, report or rumour, from fari, to speak. The root sense is what is said about a man, which is why fame in Scripture is never a possession but a report travelling ahead of someone.
biblical_def: Fame in Scripture is public report, and it is treated as a fact of providence rather than an achievement. It goes ahead of Joshua as an instrument of conquest: “So the LORD was with Joshua; and his fame was noised throughout all the country” (Joshua 6:27) — the causal order is stated plainly, the LORD was with him and therefore the report spread. It draws a foreign queen to Jerusalem for reasons that are explicitly theological: “when the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the LORD, she came to prove him with hard questions” (1 Kings 10:1) — his fame was concerning the name of the LORD, and the Lord Jesus later cites her journey to shame a generation that would not cross a street. In the Gospels fame is what gathers the crowds that the Lord Jesus then repeatedly withdraws from: “his fame went throughout all Syria: and they brought unto him all sick people” (Matthew 4:24), and after the raising of Jairus's daughter, “the fame hereof went abroad into all that land” (Matthew 9:26) — though He had charged them straitly that no man should know it. Christ is the only figure in Scripture who is shown actively suppressing His own fame, and the contrast with every ministry that cultivates it is instructive.
webster_summary: Public report. Joshua's fame follows from the LORD being with him; Solomon's fame is concerning the name of the LORD and brings a queen; and Christ's fame spreads while He repeatedly forbids the reporting of it.
webster_full: FAME, n. [L. fama; Gr. to speak.] Public report or rumor. The fame of the wisdom of Solomon.
2. Favorable report; report of good or great actions; report that exalts the character; renown; celebrity.
3. Reputation; the general estimate in which a person is held.
FAMOUS, a. Celebrated in fame or public report; renowned; much talked of and praised.
5. A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches. Prov. 22.
scriptures: Joshua 6:27
So the LORD was with Joshua; and his fame was noised throughout all the country.
1 Kings 10:1
And when the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the LORD, she came to prove him with hard questions.
Matthew 4:24

And his fame went throughout all Syria: and they brought unto him all sick people that were taken with divers diseases and torments, and those which were possessed with devils, and those which were lunatick, and those that had the palsy; and he healed them.
Proverbs 22:1
A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches, and loving favour rather than silver and gold.
corruption_summary: Fame has been converted from a report about a man into a form of capital he builds and owns — platform, following, brand — and the conversion has been imported wholesale into the ministry, where Scripture's only model actively suppresses it.
corruption_paragraphs: Every element of the modern apparatus is designed to make a man's renown into an asset he manages: the following that is counted, the platform that is built, the personal brand that is protected. Scripture's fame happens to people. Joshua's is stated as a consequence of God being with him; Solomon's is described as fame concerning the name of the LORD, so that a foreign queen arrives asking questions about God rather than about Solomon; and both are narrated as providence rather than strategy. The distinction is not that a Christian may never be known — Proverbs 22:1 says a good name is to be chosen above great riches, and 1 Timothy 3:7 requires that an overseer have a good report of them which are without. It is that a name is a trust held for the sake of what it points to, and a platform is an asset held for the sake of the man standing on it. The first can be spent; the second must be defended, and defending it is what has destroyed a great many ministries.

The most searching fact is the one the Gospels report without comment: Christ's fame spread constantly and He was constantly trying to stop it. He charges the healed leper to tell no man; He straitly charges Jairus and his wife that no man should know it; He withdraws from crowds who want to make Him a king; He forbids the disciples to say that He is the Christ. Whatever the reasons in each case — and the timing of His hour is plainly one of them — the pattern is impossible to reconcile with a ministry philosophy built on visibility. It is worth setting the ordinary evangelical assumption beside John the Baptist's: he must increase, but I must decrease, spoken by a man at the height of his own drawing power, who then lost his congregation to Christ and called it his joy fulfilled.
roots_summary: Hebrew shema (a report, what is heard) and shemuah (a rumour, tidings), both from shama, to hear; Greek pheme (a report, from phemi, to speak) and akoe (a hearing, report).
roots_lines: Hebrew shema (H8088) — a report, fame, that which is heard; the noun in Joshua 6:27 and 1 Kings 10:1.
Hebrew shama (H8085) — to hear; the root, and the first word of the Shema of Deuteronomy 6:4.
Greek pheme (G5345) — a report, fame; the word in Matthew 9:26 and Luke 4:14.
Greek akoe (G189) — a hearing, report; the word in Matthew 4:24, and in Romans 10:17, faith cometh by hearing.
Greek doxa (G1391) — glory, honour, reputation; the weightier term, which Christ says He receives not from men (John 5:41).
usage: “The LORD was with Joshua; and his fame was noised” — the causal order stated plainly.
“The fame of Solomon concerning the name of the LORD” — a report that pointed past the man.
“A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches” — a name is a trust; a platform is an asset.
